episode_thesis: Harry Krishnan argues that commodity option markets are structurally mispriced because commercial hedgers and credit-constrained end users make moderately out-of-the-money calls rich, so a long futures position at cheap curve points can have its roll cost paid by selling those calls (bounded by far calls), giving a 'virtual warehouse' that loses about a quarter of further declines and captures about two thirds of rallies, then converts to trend following once prices rise. The episode opens with his warning that the popular 0DTE short-straddle trade is a crowded, short-sample, untested-through-a-vol-spike strategy, and the host adds the trend-following view of April 2024 CTA performance and the cocoa spike.

speakers.name: Harry Krishnan
speakers.role: Guest; volatility/options manager and author, now building commodity 'virtual warehousing' structures
speakers.speaker_note: Caption attribution is clear for the long answers; the ledger assigns the COT 'blurred' question in C04 to the host.

worldview_premises.premise: Option prices are set partly by hedging necessity, not only by arbitrage, so insurance demanded by institutions or hedgers is systematically overpriced at certain strikes (moderately OTM S&P puts, moderately OTM commodity calls) while extreme strikes are not.
worldview_premises.support: Backtests across markets; institutional product flows (collars) and commercial hedging behaviour

worldview_premises.premise: Commercial hedgers (farmers, elevators, miners) sell futures into rallies because they want to stay in business, not capture the right tail, so moderate uptrends rarely accelerate.
worldview_premises.support: Research on corn and copper; stylised fact tested with backtests and statistics

worldview_premises.premise: Non-storable markets (VIX, natural gas, electricity) share the same structure: severe contango, heavy roll-down, sporadic mega spikes, so structures transfer between them.
worldview_premises.support: Analogy then backtest in his engine

worldview_premises.premise: Roll cost of a long futures position rises sharply as the price falls (curve effects), unlike physical storage cost, so cheap commodities are costly to hold via standard futures.
worldview_premises.support: Corn 2000-present: about $1 to buy and roll at a $3 price

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility is cyclical while prices trend, so paying for insurance when vol is high is worse than selling into the decline (trend following).
Every option structure encodes a regime bet; there is no structure that works in all cases, so participation should be regime-based.
Crowded, popular trades distort markets, and short-vol records in a sample with no vol spike prove little.
worldview_premises.support: Own backtests of 0DTE (Sharpe above 1 to 1.5 since 2022, only 2-3 years of data)

worldview_premises.premise: Commodity prices should rise over the medium term because of deglobalisation, green-transition metal demand, remilitarisation and weather volatility.
worldview_premises.support: Qualitative; wheat tripled in both world wars as analogy; admits technology limits grain upside

worldview_premises.premise: Demand for long-vol and trend-following strategies is cyclical: flows arrive after bad markets and dry up in long calm periods.

decision_process.practice: Run unconditional backtests across markets, check stability, identify the reason for the mispricing, then find trend- or vol-based regimes where the structure is attractive.
decision_process.why: Avoid data-mined structures; need a causal reason for the edge

decision_process.practice: A template maps the regime to one standard trade structure applied identically across markets; trend piece is systematic.
decision_process.why: No discretionary choice between put or put spread

decision_process.practice: Manual execution: legging in, time of day, sourcing liquidity.
decision_process.why: Options liquidity is sourced by hand

decision_process.practice: Only the ~10-15 most liquid commodity options markets with a storable underlying (copper, silver, gold, oil, some gas, grains; 7-8 live); cocoa, milling wheat, soybean oil excluded.
decision_process.why: Option liquidity falls sharply beyond the biggest markets; storability needed for the physical analogy

decision_process.practice: Enter cheap commodities with low-carry structure; convert to trend following after a significant rise.
decision_process.why: Capture early-rally skew at low cost, then full move with built-in exit

decision_process.practice: Bounded structure: sell moderate OTM options, buy deep OTM and ATM options; accepts losing about 25% of further declines.
decision_process.why: Upside covered, downside is a fraction

decision_process.practice: Target users: those with a long-term commodity bull view or business exposure who want pure commodity exposure at low cost, without the noise of commodity equities.
decision_process.why: Commodity equities carry hedging, diversification, passive-flow and equity-beta noise

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 25% down-capture / 2/3 up-capture / 50% spike-capture figures are rules of thumb with no stated sample, costs or period.
The corn break-even figure refers to futures-only holding; the 5-10% break-even for the structure is an aim stated hypothetically, not a result (ledger correction applied).
The switch point to trend following ('significant rise') is not defined.
The 0DTE claim that 'something is brewing' has no stated mechanism or timing; the guest also admits his own Sharpe above 1 is unreliable.
Tension: the claim that moderate OTM calls are rich because hedgers sell futures into rallies mixes two different channels (futures selling versus option buying by end users).
Uranium vehicles may not give true storage-equivalent exposure; hedging 'necessity' claim relies on backtests only.
Execution is manual and the universe is only 7-8 markets, limiting scale and replicability.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Guest's inputs: commodity price level (cheap vs history), shape of the futures curve (roll cost), call-versus-put skew and richness of moderate OTM calls, commercial hedger positioning, option liquidity, and for vol, the term-structure kink at the short end and open interest in 0DTE. Horizon is medium to long term (months to years) for commodities; 0DTE risk is unspecified. Host inputs: trend signals and the trend barometer, central bank divergence for FX trends.
reader_inferences: (reader) The structure is effectively a short-call-spread overlay on a long futures position, so its edge depends on moderate calls being rich relative to realized outcomes; if hedging demand shrinks, the edge goes with it.
(reader) The hybrid (value then trend) approach inherits both strategies' regime risk; the claimed 'regime-conditional' templates were fitted on historical data without disclosed out-of-sample tests.
(reader) The guest's own caution on 0DTE (short sample, no vol event) applies equally to commodity backtests that include few spike episodes.
(reader) The host's disagreement on cocoa positioning shows that COT categories cannot reliably separate trend followers from other speculators.
